units.text: After arrival: families follow, and a prayer for the city
What do the first days of settlement look like in the accounts of families, a newborn, and fever?

After arrival, other sides of the migration began to unfold: migrants followed one another to Medina, some family members arrived later, and Asma recounted the birth of her son at Quba. Aisha’s account mentions Abu Bakr and Bilal falling ill and the Prophet’s ﷺ prayer for Medina. We read these scenes alongside one another without imposing a single date on them.

The narrative of Ibn Hibban, the account of Asma, and Ibn Hajar’s explanations differ in voice and precision: each says what falls within its own scope, and a commentary or marginal note does not become the eyewitness testimony of the woman concerned.
Arrivals from Mecca

Arrival did not close the door on migration. Ibn Ishaq relates that the migrants arrived one after another, excepting from his statement about those who remained in Mecca people subjected to trial and people held captive. His account depicts houses left closed when their occupants departed, not a picture that requires every migrant to have left with family and property.

Then comes the account of families arriving from Mecca. Ibn Hibban relates that Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Rafi were sent to bring Sawda and the Prophet’s ﷺ daughters, and that Abu Bakr sent Ibn Urayqit to his son Abd Allah to have him come with his family. In this account the families make a further journey after the arrival; the line does not tell us the names of everyone who came.

Ibn Hajar, citing Ibn Ishaq, adds names of those who arrived with the Prophet’s ﷺ family and Abu Bakr’s household; he then mentions Ruqayya’s earlier arrival with Uthman and Zaynab’s later arrival. In Ibn Sad’s account, by contrast, the Prophet ﷺ sends Zayd and Abu Rafi from Abu Ayyub’s house to Mecca, and they return with some of his family. The details in one of these texts do not become a list that Ibn Hibban explicitly gave when he said “his daughters.”
In the account of brotherhood

Alongside the arrival of families, the account of brotherhood appears in Ibn Hibban’s narrative: it is preceded by a gathering of those invited, followed by words attributed to the Prophet ﷺ and mention of those he paired as brothers. It is a long narrative bounded here by the limits of its pages; the author does not provide a new chain of transmission for it at this point. Its wording and names should therefore be read as they stand, not as a comprehensive ruling on every pairing of brothers.

In the continuation of this narrative Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf is named with Uthman. The Sad named there, however, is Sad ibn Abi Waqqas with Ammar; the reader does not find here an account of Abd al-Rahman’s brotherhood with Sad ibn al-Rabi or their conversation. That story is left aside until the text that actually relates it is opened, rather than filling the gap with something absent from this text.
Asma and the newborn at Quba

From the account of the families we turn to a newborn brought to the Prophet ﷺ: Asma bint Abi Bakr relates that she set out at the end of her pregnancy, stopped at Quba and gave birth there to Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, then brought him to the Prophet ﷺ. He chewed a date, rubbed it on the baby’s palate, prayed for him and blessed him. Bukhari’s suspended follow-up report adds that she migrated while pregnant, without repeating the details of this encounter.

Aisha tells the scene in a shorter account, mentioning the date and the Prophet’s ﷺ saliva. Her abridgment is not a different date of birth; what Asma says about Quba remains her own testimony, and we cannot infer a day or month of birth from the order of the sentences.
Fever, longing, and prayer

Arrival did not bring good health to everyone. Aisha describes the illness of Abu Bakr and Bilal: Abu Bakr has a verse about death’s nearness, while Bilal has two lines lamenting the valley, idhkhir grass, jalil, the waters of Majanna, and Shama and Tafil. Abu Bakr thus mentioned the nearness of death, and Bilal’s poetry expressed longing; neither of their statements was the Prophet’s ﷺ prayer.

Aisha brought news of the illness to the Prophet ﷺ, who prayed for love of Medina, its health, blessing in its sa and mudd measures, and the transfer of its fever to al-Juhfa. Sahih Muslim condenses the account to the two men’s complaint and the prayer, while Bukhari has a different wording of the prayer. These varying formulations give us views of the account, not grounds for counting separate fever episodes.
Names of those who arrived and the limits of the narrative

Ibn Hibban’s selected text speaks of a mission to Mecca and Abu Bakr’s family setting out; Ibn Hajar’s citation of Ibn Ishaq gives more names, followed by Ibn Hajar’s comment on the timing of Abd Allah’s birth. Ibn Sad’s report mentions lodging those who arrived in Haritha ibn al-Numan’s house. We treat these as distinct limits of narration, not as one list imposed on every witness.

Because this reading concerns what followed the arrival, the accounts of the families, brotherhood, the newborn and the fever are placed after the mosque chapter. That is the order of the chapter, not a dating of all the events. Ibn Hajar reports that some family members arrived while the Prophet ﷺ was building his mosque; that does not establish that every incident here occurred after the building was finished.
What does Asma’s account establish?

Asma’s wording preserves her pregnancy on departure, her delivery at Quba and her subsequent bringing of the child to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Hajar explains the word mutimm (“at term”) in her account and says that her stopping at Quba does not mean that she arrived before the Prophet ﷺ moved on from there.

Ibn Hajar favors the first year, disagreeing with the dating to the second year, after twenty months, attributed to al-Waqidi; he then objects to such a long interval, citing the migration of Abu Bakr’s household. This is a commentator’s preference and a discussion of different reports, not a calendar date spoken in Asma’s hadith. He limits the sense in which the child is called the “first” to the migrants in Medina, and mentions other names outside that scope.
Where the poetry belongs, and the voices of commentary

Majanna, Shama and Tafil occur in Bilal’s verse expressing longing for Mecca. Ibn Hajar explains the first as a place near Mecca and reports differing descriptions of the other two. Al-Juhfa does not appear in Bilal’s verses here; it appears instead in the Prophet’s ﷺ prayer to transfer the fever.

Ibn Hajar also transmits an addition from Ibn Ishaq in which Aisha asks Amir ibn Fuhayra a question and he responds in verse; he then mentions another, interrupted chain for the addition. The poet’s line about an old custom for warding off an epidemic, however, belongs in Ibn Hajar’s commentary, not in the poetry of Abu Bakr or Bilal.

A note accompanying Muslim explains the description of Medina as afflicted by an epidemic and cites remarks by al-Khattabi and others, and al-Nawawi, about al-Juhfa. These are judgments reported in the note, not a continuation of the prayer; Aisha’s words and what she attributes to the Prophet ﷺ remain distinct from them.

The Messenger of God ﷺ sent Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Rafi from Abu Ayyub’s house to Mecca, giving them two camels and five hundred dirhams. They returned to him with Fatima and Umm Kulthum, the Messenger of God’s ﷺ daughters, his wife Sawda bint Zama, and Usama ibn Zayd. The Messenger of God’s ﷺ daughter Ruqayya had already been taken away in migration by her husband Uthman ibn Affan; Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi kept back his wife Zaynab, the Messenger of God’s ﷺ daughter. Zayd ibn Haritha brought his wife Umm Ayman with her son Usama ibn Zayd. Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr set out with them, with Abu Bakr’s family, including Aisha. They came to Medina, where he lodged them in Haritha ibn al-Numan’s house (4).
